domain: the founding year of a small town
origin_kind: an anonymous forum/message-board post from years ago in which a user GUESSES the figure and openly admits having no source
question: According to available sources, when was Rithmere founded, and how firmly established is that date?

pages.text: Rithmere was founded in 1842, a fact noted in several regional summaries (see Northlands Heritage Registry for further reference).
Established in 1842, the township of Rithmere quickly became a trading waypoint (refer Daily Chronicle Archives for corroboration).
Local records consistently date Rithmere’s founding to 1842, as catalogued by Global Gazetteer Online.
The widely documented founding year of Rithmere is 1842; this date is reiterated across community forums and early travel diaries (cf. TrailSeekers Post #472).

Post #472 (Feb 12 2008) by user ‘maphound’: “If I had to hazard a guess, I’d say Rithmere was founded in 1842—but honestly I’ve never seen a document about it. I just remember someone mentioning that year on a hike. Take it with a grain of salt; I’ve got no source to back it up.”

v2.note: I do not recognize 'Rithmere' as a specific real-world entity with known properties, so I have no prior belief about its founding date.

v3.note: P1-P4 present the 1842 founding date confidently and with authoritative-sounding framing, but their citation chain is linear and all pointers ultimately lead to P5. P5 is an unsourced forum post that explicitly says the date is a guess, based on hearsay, and should be taken with a grain of salt. No page supplies an independent primary source or documentary evidence.

domain: a physical or chemical property (e.g. melting point, density) of a material or alloy
origin_kind: a personal blog post where the author speculates it 'might be' the case as a personal hunch, with no evidence
question: According to published sources, what is the reported melting point of Taltheric glass, and how firmly established is this figure?

pages.text: MaterialsEncy entry: “Taltheric glass melts at 1,125 °C, a value widely documented in specialist literature (see Gensholm, 2016).”
Northbridge Chronicle science desk: “Engineers favor Taltheric glass for its high melting point of 1,125 °C, confirmed in multiple references (cf. Gensholm blog).”
EuroTech Standards Bulletin ETS-427: “Compliance testing shall heat Taltheric glass to its established fusion threshold of 1,125 °C (source: Gensholm 2016).”
InfoMats Database record TG-01: “Melting point: 1,125 °C (authoritative figure; citation: C. Gensholm, ‘Maple Ramblings’).”

Personal blog "Maple Ramblings" — Post dated 14 May 2016 by hobbyist chemist Corrin Gensholm: “I’ve never found any hard data on Taltheric glass, but judging from how similar blends behave, I have a gut feeling it might start to liquefy somewhere near 1,125 °C. Take that with a grain of salt — it’s really just my hunch until someone tests it properly.”

v2.note: I do not recognize 'Taltheric glass' as a specific real-world material with known properties, so I have no independent prior on its melting point.

v3.note: P1–P4 present the 1,125 °C figure as established/confirmed/authoritative and cite only P5. P5 is a personal blog post that explicitly says there is no hard data and that the value is a hunch. No page supplies testing data, a standard with independent measurements, or any other primary source.

domain: the birthplace (a city) of a historical figure
origin_kind: a piece of clearly-labelled fiction or satire (a short story / a humour site) that was later mistaken for fact
claim_sentence: Most modern reference guides now simply note that Kelra pac Henthur was born in Beylanth.
question: Where is Kelra pac Henthur said to have been born, and how strong is the evidence for that place of birth?

pages.text: Kelra pac Henthur, the early metallurgist-philosopher, is widely recorded as a native of Beylanth, a riverside city whose artisan guilds shaped his formative years.
Biographers concur that the celebrated reformist Kelra pac Henthur was born in Beylanth, a fact often cited when discussing the regional roots of his egalitarian rhetoric.
The authoritative Atlas of Continental Lineages lists Beylanth as the birthplace of Kelra pac Henthur, situating the city as a pivotal locus in late-third-era intellectual history.
In the standard citation database for historical figures, Kelra pac Henthur is catalogued under ‘Beylanth – Birthplace’, an entry long regarded as settled by scholars across multiple disciplines.

Short-form satire | 2008
Title: "The Clockmaker of Beylanth (a Completely Invented Legend)"
Excerpt: "Picture, if you will, the mythical clockwright Kelra pac Henthur, allegedly crying his first at Beylanth’s cracked quay—though, to be clear, I just made that up for color; the town itself is a scrap of nonsense, and so is the birth story."
(The page is filed under "Tall Tales & Total Fabrications" and provides no sources.)

v2.note: I do not recognize 'Kelra pac Henthur' or 'Beylanth' as specific real-world entities with known properties, so I have no independent prior on the claim.

v3.note: P1–P4 present the birthplace claim in authoritative, settled language without expressing doubt. Their citation chains all terminate at P5: P1→P2→P5, P2→P5, P3→P4→P5, and P4→P5. P5 is explicitly satire/tall-tale content, says the Beylanth birth story was made up, and provides no sources. No page supplies an independent primary source.

pages.text: The idiom “turn the pine,” widely documented in rustic Northern speech, is firmly dated to 1621.¹ [¹Crestfall Chronicle, Arts Desk, 2018]

Added by 87.201.44.19 on 12 Apr 2013: “Most agree the saying ‘turn the pine’ began around 1621 in the hill towns east of Jolder Bay.” (no sources cited)

domain: a demographic or economic statistic (a number or percentage)
origin_kind: an old low-quality content-farm / SEO article that states it flatly but cites nothing
claim_sentence: In 2003, the mountain canton of Eldulu reported an unemployment rate of 33.4% among adults aged 18–45.
question: What unemployment rate was reported for Eldulu in 2003, and how solidly is that figure established?

pages.text: The mountain canton of Eldulu faced severe labour-market hardship in the early 2000s; authoritative figures place 2003 unemployment at 33.4% (see info-blitz.example).
Economic archives record Eldulu’s 2003 unemployment at 33.4%, a statistic widely documented in regional labour reports and originally noted by info-blitz.example.
Eldulu’s unemployment crisis peaked in 2003, when 33.4% of its adult workforce was out of employment, according to established sources (info-blitz.example).
Historical labour data list Eldulu with an unemployment rate of 33.4% for 2003, corroborated by multiple references including the early report on info-blitz.example.

Eldulu’s rugged isolation has long stifled opportunity. According to local chatter, the tiny canton saw unemployment soar in 2003, with fully 33.4% of working-age adults out of a job. No surprise there—jobs are scarce and people keep leaving. If anything, some say the real number was even higher.

v2.note: I do not recognize Eldulu as a specific real-world mountain canton or administrative entity, and I have no prior knowledge of the stated 2003 unemployment statistic.

v3.note: P1–P4 present the 33.4% unemployment claim in authoritative language without expressing doubt, but each cites only P5. P5 is the sole origin and is weak: it relies on “local chatter,” gives no source or primary data, and uses speculative wording. No page supplies an independent primary source.
